blocks.heading: A set of business-size indicators
blocks.text: Business size can be described through legal form of ownership, nature of business, nature of product, capital employed, total assets, number of employees, level of technology, market share, turnover, profitability and value of output. Two straightforward numerical measures are the number of employees and annual turnover. No single indicator ranks every business fairly. A highly automated producer may employ fewer people than a labour-intensive workshop but produce much more. Some indicators are descriptive clues, such as ownership form or technology, rather than a numerical scale. Others measure different things: turnover is sales revenue, profit is the surplus after costs, and total assets is the value of resources owned. Select a measure suited to the comparison and state the time period or valuation basis. Compare similar activities where possible and use several indicators if they disagree. Large does not necessarily mean successful, profitable or well managed. A small specialist may earn a high profit relative to its investment, while a large producer can make a loss.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Two furniture businesses each employ ten people. Tuli Furnishings has automated machinery and much higher annual sales than hand-finishing workshop Tameka Joinery. Employee count alone makes them look equal. Turnover and assets reveal differences in the scale of their operations, while neither measure by itself tells us whose customers are more satisfied.

blocks.heading: Legal form of ownership
blocks.text: Legal form identifies how a business is owned and organised, such as a sole trader, partnership or company. It is a descriptive clue to size because some company forms may make larger funding possible. Its limitation is that the form does not specify actual sales, employees or assets: a company can be small and a long-established individually owned business can be substantial.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Eha Bakery is a company employing two people; a nearby sole trader employs eight. The company label alone does not make Eha larger. Compare employee numbers or sales for the same period as well.

blocks.heading: Nature of business
blocks.text: Nature of business identifies the activity undertaken, such as mining, retailing or personal services. It helps choose meaningful size comparisons: mining often needs extensive equipment, while a personal service may depend mainly on labour. Its limitation is that activity is a category, not a measured quantity. A retailer is not automatically larger or smaller than a manufacturer.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A sewing workshop and a mineral-extraction site each employ twenty people. Equal employment can hide very different investment needs. The activity helps interpret asset figures but cannot itself give an exact size ranking.

blocks.heading: Nature of product
blocks.text: Nature of product describes what is supplied and its characteristics, such as a low-priced standard item or a high-value customised item. It helps explain why units of output can be misleading. Its limitation is that the kind or price of product does not alone establish the business’s total scale. One expensive item and many inexpensive items require a comparable monetary measure.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A boat builder completes three custom boats while a bakery makes thousands of rolls. Counting physical items alone would heavily favour the bakery. Compare annual value of output and investment alongside the nature of the products.

blocks.heading: Capital employed
blocks.text: Capital employed is the long-term finance used in a business, commonly measured as owners’ capital plus non-current liabilities, or total assets less current liabilities. A larger amount can indicate a greater scale of resources committed. Its limitation is that capital-intensive and labour-intensive activities need different investment, so it does not translate directly into jobs or sales. Use a consistent accounting basis.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Oruvatu Milling uses substantial machinery, while a tutoring enterprise works mainly through its staff. More capital employed at the mill would indicate more finance tied into its operation, not necessarily more employees or a higher return. Capital employed is a money amount, not the count of workers.

blocks.heading: Total assets
blocks.text: Total assets is the recorded value of all assets controlled by the business, including non-current and current assets. It indicates the resource base used to operate. Its limitation is that valuation dates and methods, the age of equipment and renting rather than owning premises can distort comparisons. A business with expensive assets may use them poorly or sell little output.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: One transport firm owns its vehicles; another rents an equally capable fleet. The owner may record more assets even when both carry similar loads. Asset values should therefore be interpreted with capacity and turnover, rather than treated as a complete measure of activity.

blocks.heading: Number of employees
blocks.text: Number of employees measures the size of the workforce. It is straightforward and useful for comparing labour use in similar businesses. Its limitation is that automation and differing part-time hours make headcounts less comparable. A highly mechanised producer can have fewer workers but far more output. Where hours differ, compare equivalent working time rather than ignoring the difference.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A machine-equipped packaging business has six full-time workers and a manual packer has twelve. The second has the larger workforce. That does not establish larger output without knowing working hours and productivity. Do not change the question from employment size to overall success.

blocks.heading: Level of technology
blocks.text: Level of technology describes how advanced or extensive equipment and methods are. It can help explain productive capacity and why output is high with relatively few workers. Its limitation is that sophisticated equipment is a qualitative clue rather than a complete size measure: one advanced machine can belong to a small specialist. Underused technology need not produce large sales.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A small engraver owns a computer-controlled cutting machine but completes only a few orders each week. Its advanced equipment does not make it larger than every manual workshop. Check capacity used and annual output before drawing that conclusion.

blocks.heading: Market share
blocks.text: Market share is a business’s sales as a proportion of total sales in a defined market over a stated period. Use the same basis, such as sales value for both business and market. It indicates relative presence among competitors. Its limitation is that the market boundary matters: a large share of a tiny town market can represent fewer sales than a small share of a national market.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tula Bread has half of a small settlement’s bread sales; another bakery has one tenth of a much larger regional market. Tula has the higher percentage in its defined market, but the other bakery may sell more bread. State the market before using market share to infer scale.

blocks.heading: Turnover
blocks.text: Turnover is sales revenue over a period. It indicates the monetary volume of sales and makes comparison of unlike products more useful than a physical unit count. Its limitation is that prices and the period covered affect it, and high revenue does not guarantee profit. A firm buying expensive goods for resale can have high turnover but a thin surplus after costs.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Kavesa Shop has annual sales revenue of N$900,000; a repairer reports annual profit of N$100,000. These figures cannot rank turnover because the repairer’s figure is profit. Obtain its annual sales revenue first. Revenue and profit are different measures.

blocks.heading: Profitability
blocks.text: Profitability concerns the ability to generate profit relative to a relevant base such as sales or capital employed. It can help compare financial performance, but its limitation as a size indicator is that efficiency or a high margin is not the same as large operations. Absolute profit is the surplus after costs; a profitability ratio relates that surplus to another figure. Neither proves large employment or assets.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A small specialist keeps a greater proportion of each N$1 of sales as profit than a large discount store. The specialist may be more profitable relative to sales while remaining smaller in turnover and staff. State the basis of comparison instead of equating a high percentage with a large enterprise.

blocks.heading: Value of output
blocks.text: Value of output measures production in monetary terms over a period. It allows outputs of different kinds or sizes to be expressed on a common money basis. Its limitation is that changing prices and different valuation methods affect the result, and produced goods may remain unsold. Therefore value of output is not automatically the same as turnover, which relates to sales.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A workshop makes furniture in December but sells some of it in January. December’s production value includes furniture still held at the period end, while December turnover includes only sales made in that period. Use matching periods and distinguish output from sales.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Small-firm survival and sector/size distinctions
blocks.text:
Omila Shade near Outjo makes customised garden shades from purchased fabric. It has three employees and a small rented workshop. A large supplier sells standard shades. Local households choose Omila for unusual sizes, and orders are sufficient for its present three-person operation. Omila could rent a bigger factory and concentrate on identical shades, but there is no firm demand for those extra units. For part (b) only, a guesthouse group now commits to a two-year order for identical shades sufficient to keep the proposed larger factory busy. All other facts are unchanged.

a Evaluate remaining small and customised under the original facts. Classify Omila’s activity and explain why one size measure alone is insufficient. [12]
b Evaluate the same choice after the stated guesthouse order arrives. Explain whether the original recommendation should change. [12]

a Omila manufactures shades and is secondary. Three employees describe workforce size but omit productive equipment, sales and the high value of customised products. Its present demand fits a small operation; unusual sizes and personal attention distinguish it from the large standard supplier. Expanding might allow more output, yet the bigger factory would create commitments before demand is established. Remain small because the niche is proven for current scale whereas the standard market is not. This judgement would weaken if dependable standard orders emerged. b The two-year order changes demand certainty, not the fact that manufacturing is secondary. Expansion can now use the larger factory for a specified customer rather than speculative stock; standardisation may reduce unit costs if the order uses capacity efficiently and coordination is controlled. Against this, reliance on one guesthouse group creates risk at contract end and the larger operation could displace custom work. Shift towards the larger operation only after checking that the agreed order covers its extra commitments and can be delivered with the resources available. The recommendation becomes more favourable to expansion because dependable demand replaces the original uncertainty, while renewal and customer dependence remain reasons to limit longer commitments.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Small-firm survival and sector/size distinctions
blocks.text:
Nareta Repairs in Mariental employs four people and repairs customers’ bicycles. It buys replacement parts from a manufacturer. A large retailer nearby sells standard bicycles but offers no repairs. Nareta earns most of its revenue from individual repair jobs and can discuss each problem directly with its customer. Its owner is considering replacing that personal service with a much larger standard bicycle assembly operation. No firm order for assembled bicycles exists.

a Explain why turnover and employee numbers might rank the repair business and the parts manufacturer differently. In your answer distinguish their activity sectors. [8]
b Evaluate whether the small repair firm is likely to survive alongside the large retailer if it keeps its present focus. [12]

a Repairs provide a tertiary service while the parts manufacturer transforms inputs in the secondary sector. Employee numbers measure labour use, whereas turnover measures sales revenue over a period. Repair jobs require direct labour and discussion; an automated manufacturer may sell a large volume with few staff. The manufacturer could therefore have higher turnover despite similar or lower headcount. Different prices also influence turnover, so sales value alone cannot establish physical output. Compare the same accounting period and use both indicators with relevant information about activity. b A small firm can survive where a niche and personal service provide enough paid demand to cover costs. Nareta fills the retailer’s stated repair gap, understands individual faults and can encourage repeat custom. Remaining small avoids committing to unconfirmed assembly demand. However, four people limit the number of repairs that can be handled, and dependence on individual jobs may leave revenue variable; the retailer could later introduce a competing service. Survival is plausible, not assured. Retain and monitor the repair focus while demand covers operating costs; this recommendation rests on the service gap, not on an assumption that every small business can undercut a large one. Reassess if repair revenue falls or a larger service contract appears.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Small-firm survival and sector/size distinctions
blocks.text:
Nareta Repairs in Mariental employs four people and repairs customers’ bicycles. It buys replacement parts from a manufacturer. A large retailer nearby sells standard bicycles but offers no repairs. Nareta earns most of its revenue from individual repair jobs and can discuss each problem directly with its customer. Its owner is considering replacing that personal service with a much larger standard bicycle assembly operation. No firm order for assembled bicycles exists.

a(i) Define a primary-sector business. [2]
a(ii) State two reasons small firms may survive alongside large rivals. [2]
b State the activity sector of Nareta’s repair service and the activity sector of its parts manufacturer. [2]
c Explain two limitations of using employee numbers alone to compare Nareta with a highly automated parts manufacturer. [6]
d Evaluate whether Nareta should replace its personal repair service with large-scale assembly now. [8]

a(i) A business that obtains natural resources, for example through farming or extraction. a(ii) Personal customer service and serving a specialist niche. b Repairs are tertiary; manufacturing replacement parts is secondary. c Automation allows the manufacturer to produce many parts with relatively few employees, so headcount understates its output compared with labour-intensive repairs. Employee count also omits investment in machinery: two firms could have the same workforce yet very different assets and productive capacity. Use employee numbers alongside turnover and asset or output measures for the same period. d Personal service meets a gap the retailer leaves and uses Nareta’s direct contact with each customer, supporting repeat repair demand. Larger assembly could increase output and could lower unit costs if sufficient standard orders use the capacity, but there are no firm orders and Nareta could lose its repair niche while committing to larger costs. Keep the repair focus now; reconsider expansion after testing demand, rather than treating size itself as the objective.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Small-firm survival and sector/size distinctions
blocks.text:
Omila Shade near Outjo makes customised garden shades from purchased fabric. It has three employees and a small rented workshop. A large supplier sells standard shades. Local households choose Omila for unusual sizes, and orders are sufficient for its present three-person operation. Omila could rent a bigger factory and concentrate on identical shades, but there is no firm demand for those extra units.

Evaluate the decision to keep Omila Shade small rather than move immediately to the larger standard-shade factory. Give a concise answer plan, using activity sector and suitable size measures. [12]

Opening: Omila is secondary because it transforms fabric into shades. Size should be assessed using employees alongside turnover, assets or output; custom products and standard products make physical counts alone misleading. Case for staying small: unusual sizes give a niche that standard suppliers do not serve; three staff and direct customer contact support adaptation without a speculative factory commitment. Case for expansion: standardisation could serve a larger market and reduce unit costs if sufficient sales keep capacity used, but current facts do not establish that demand. Judgement: remain with the custom niche now because present orders support it while extra standard orders are uncertain. Review verified orders and capacity before growing; a larger premises count alone is not evidence of better performance.
